name: Arvanitika

ancestors.notes: Arvanitika descends from medieval Tosk Albanian, brought to southern Greece by Albanian settlers from the 13th-14th centuries; it preserves consonant clusters simplified in the modern standard, e.g. gljuhë /ˈɡʎuxə/ ('language') vs standard gjuhë /ˈɟuhə/ (Wikipedia: Arvanitika).

Centuries of bilingualism with Greek in Attica/Boeotia/Peloponnese produced lexical and phonological influence on Arvanitika (Wikipedia: Arvanitika, on the sociolinguistic contact situation). NOTE: the previously-cited example pair (haristis/dhrom) was mis-sourced on re-verification: the Arvanitika Wikipedia article attributes those specific loans to Italian Arbëresh speakers descended from Arvanite settlers, not to Arvanitika itself, so they have been removed rather than kept unsupported.

notes: STUB: no reliable, sourced grapheme-to-IPA table found this session. Arvanitika has no standardized orthography: it has historically been written in the Greek alphabet (often with added letters b, d, e, j or diacritics — e.g. Γ̇/γ̇ for /ɟ/, Λ̇/λ̇ for /ʎ/, Σ̈/σ̈ for /ʃ/, per Wikipedia) and, less often and inconsistently, in a Latin alphabet; Sasse (1991) documents eleven dialect groups with no convergence toward a common written standard, and Arvanites are generally not literate in the Latin-based standard Albanian orthography either. Per AGENTS.md, an inventory must not be fabricated and a non-Latin-script language must not be given an invented Latin placeholder; graphemes is left empty pending a sourced per-dialect table (e.g. from Sasse 1991 or a Greek-script primer). script is set to Greek as the historically primary system; this is a design decision, not an assertion that Arvanitika has a single fixed alphabet.

sources.author: Sasse, Hans-Jürgen
